NATIONAL COMPANY LAW APPELLATE TRIBUNAL
PRINCIPAL BENCH, NEW DELHI

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1766 of 2024
&
I.A. No. 6443, 6445 of 2024
[Arising out of the Impugned Order dated 11.06.2024 passed by the
Adjudicating Authority, National Company Law Tribunal, Ahmedabad
Bench in I.A. No. 350 of 2021 filed in C.P.(IB) No. 397 of 2018]

IN THE MATTER OF:

Narayan Ramchandra Ghumatkar
Suspended Director of KSL & INDUSTRIES LTD.
1/19, N M JOSHI MARG, BYCULLA STATION WEST,
MUMBAI – 400027

...Appellant

Versus

KIRAN SHAH
RESOLUTION PROFESSIONAL, KSL & INDUSTRIES LTD.
608, SAKAR-1, NEAR GANDHIGRAM RAILWAY STATION,
ASHRAM ROAD, AHMEDABAD – 380 009
Email: dhruvvitks@gmail.com

...Respondent

Present:

For Appellant(s)
: Mr. K.D. Sharma, Advocate.

For Respondent(s) : CA Kiran Shah, Respondent in person.

J U D G M E N T
(Hybrid Mode)

[Per: Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Member (Judicial)]
The facts, that require inevitable consideration are, that the Appellant,
who happens to be the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor ‘KSL &
Industries Ltd.’, has challenged the impugned order dated 11.06.2024, that
was passed by the Ld. NCLT while considering I.A. No. 350 of 2021 filed by
the Resolution Professional, thereby invoking the provisions contained under
Section 19(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

2 of 18

2.
The brief facts, as referred to by the Ld. Counsel for the Appellant for
challenging the impugned order dated 11.06.2024, could be summarized in
the following manner. The CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor
M/s KSL & Industries Ltd., by initiation of the same, by an order has been
passed on 06.09.2019. As a consequence of the initiation of the CIRP and RP
was appointed, namely Mr. Kiran Shah, the Respondent herein, by the Ld.
Adjudicating Authority vide its order of 28.07.2020.
3.
It is the case of the Appellant that ever since the initiation of the CIRP
w.e.f. 06.09.2019, the Appellant had been rendering his fullest cooperation,
along with the Suspended Board of Directors, as regards to supplying of all
details in form of numerous emails, series of records, documentation and
information as was shared by the Suspended Directors with the Resolution
Professional, those were expressed to be required to be considered for the
purposes of carrying out the CIRP.
4.
During the intervening period, one of the Directors, namely Smt. Mansi
Wadkar, Respondent No.1(a) before the Adjudicating Authority, who was the
lead director of the Corporate Debtor and was mostly at the helm of affairs of
the Corporate Debtor, was intricately aware of all the financial transactions
and details of it, that were carried out by the Corporate Debtor and she had
been effectively and actively collaborating too with the Resolution Professional
by providing all requisite information from time to time including the
documents. But unfortunately, Smt. Mansi Wadkar met with sad demise
passed away on 02.05.2021. Upon her demise, the other Suspended Directors

3 of 18

including the Appellant had very limited information available with them, that
could be provided to the Resolution Professional because most of the
knowledge vested and held with Late Smt. Mansi Wadkar. Though, despite of
the best of the efforts, the Appellant contends, that still as and when the
information was solicited by the Resolution Professional, he had supplied the
requisite information, but still the Resolution Professional being dissatisfied
with the information supplied by the Appellant, is said to have filed an
application I.A. no. 350 of 2021, by filing the same before the Registry of the
NCLT under Section 19(2) of the I&B Code, to be read with Section 60(5). In
the application thus preferred, the Resolution Professional had came up with
the case, that upon the CIRP being initiated against M/s ‘KSL & Industries
Ltd.’, the Company which according to him was incorporated under the
provisions of Companies Act, 1956, that was placed under the CIRP and
during its course, number of vital information were required to be solicited
and as such. He submitted that Mr. Anil Kumar, the Opposite Party No.2 in
the Company Petition, after being appointed as such as an IRP, proceeded
with the CIRP but could not be completed because of which an extension was
granted for completion of CIRP by an order dated 04.03.2020.
5.
The Respondent’s case has been that the Ld. Adjudicating Authority
while exercising its power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, appointed the
applicant to the I.A., i.e., the Respondent No.1 herein, Kiran Shah, as a
Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor vide its order dated
28.07.2020. The Respondent No.2 is shown to have filed an application, for

4 of 18

grant of further extension and for extension of CIRP period beyond 330 days.
Owing to the fact, that in the application for exhaustion of time it was alleged
by the Resolution Professional, that it was becoming very difficult to complete
the CIRP in respect of the Corporate Debtor. The reason was due to the
situation that was prevailing on account of persistent dispute amongst the
members of the CoC. Taking into cognizance of the entire scenario, the Ld.
Adjudicating Authority is shown to have granted an extension of 233 days
vide its order dated 24.11.2020, to complete the CIRP.
6.
It has been the case of the Resolution Professional, that henceforth,
several meetings with the CoC were held, holding discussions with regard to
several vital matters having an impact upon the revival of the Corporate
Debtor and for the purposes of completion of the CIRP. The applicant to I.A.
No. 350 of 2021, i.e., the Respondent No.1, in an application thus preferred
had submitted that O.P. No.1, i.e., the present Appellant, since being the
representative of the Suspended Management of the Corporate Debtor, has
not submitted the complete records. Those were demanded and required to
be maintained under the Companies Act and other documents prepared
under various other laws as applicable, statutorily required, viz, the registers
like fixed assets register; titled documents of the properties of the Corporate
Debtor, employees record and such other documents and data, which were
duly mandated and required to be submitted under the I&B Code, for an
effective completion of the CIRP. It is alleged by the Applicant/Respondent,
that when despite various reminders and several telephonic communications

5 of 18

and email sent by Respondent No.1 along with the list of pending data and
documents, those were required, they were not supplied.
7.
It had been the case of the Respondent, that owing to the aforesaid fact
of incomplete information supplied, he was constrained to hold the 6th
meeting of the members of the CoC, which was held on 01.01.2021, wherein
the issue of pending details and data from the Suspended Management was
also discussed, in the CoC meeting it was alleged, that the Appellant had
agreed to furnish the pending details and data as were required by
Respondent No.1. In relation thereto to substantiate the application, the
Respondents have made reference to the minutes of the meeting of the CoC,
that was placed on record.
8.
It is on this background the Respondent No.1 submitted that the
conduct of the Appellant was demonstrative of a non-cooperative attitude of
the Appellant, which was prejudicial to the interest of the stakeholders of the
Corporate Debtor, besides that it also reflected the negligence and
irresponsible behaviour of the Suspended Management of the Corporate
Debtor. The allegation levelled in the application was that despite several
reminders over calls and emails, the Respondent No.1’s emails and
particularly the email dated 27.03.2021 calling to give the elaborative list of
documents, which were still pending, they were not supplied. Which was
taken to be an act of non-cooperation on the part of the Appellant in
disrupting and holding the continuing the CIRP in respect of the Corporate
Debtor.

6 of 18

9.
It is the case of the Respondent in the I.A. thus filed before the Ld.
Tribunal invoking Section 19(2) of the I&B Code, that after being appointed
as the Resolution Professional, he had requested the erstwhile Resolution
Professional, to hand over the possession of the Corporate Debtor, as well as
the records, vide its email communication dated 31.07.2020, however in that
process of handing over the records by the Erstwhile IRP, the O.P. No.2 to the
I.A., didn’t remain present at the corporate office of the Corporate Debtor,
where part of the records were stated to be maintained by the Applicant. The
Respondent No.1 submitted that despite the email communication that was
made as part of the application, the records were not submitted, he preferred
the I.A. praying for the following reliefs:

“6.1. The Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority may be pleased to
direct the Opponent No. 1 herein, being the representatives of the
Suspended Management of the Corporate Debtor, to co-operate
with the Resolution Professional, the Applicant herein and direct to
submit the documents and data as sought for in the Annexure E
(Colly.) and support / co-operate as and when required by the
Resolution Professional, the Applicant herein.

6.2. The Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority may be pleased to direct
the erstwhile Interim resolution Professional, Opponent No. 2
herein to co-operate with the Resolution Professional, the Applicant
herein and direct to submit the documents and data as sought for
in the Annexure H and support as and when required by the
Resolution Professional, the Applicant herein.

6.3. The Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority may be pleased to grant
such other and further reliefs as may be deemed fit and proper by
this Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority, in the interest of equity and
justice.”

7 of 18

10.
Particularly in relation to the subject falling to be brought under Section
19(2) of the Code. The Respondent along with the application has filed
Annexure-E, which according to him contained the list of documents that
were required to be submitted, the particulars of which constituted as to be
part of the application, are extracted hereunder:

8 of 18

11.
When this application came up for consideration, the Appellant is
shown to have filed a reply, in the shape of a compliance affidavit, on
04.06.2023 in response to the said I.A., the applicant contended therein that
he happens to be one of the Directors whose Board had been suspended in
his capacity vide order dated 06.09.2019 by the order of the Tribunal, that
was passed in C.P.(IB) No. 397 of 2018 and in the response affidavit filed on
04.06.2023 by the Appellant. Apart from denying the allegations in I.A. No.
350 of 2021 filed by the Respondent and placing on record the fact that during
the intervening period between 08.06.2022 to 15.09.2022, the Appellant
contends, that he did provide the required information as per Section 19 of
the I&B Code, and the following documents were supplied by the Appellant to
the RP.

(i) Complete status of cases against the Corporate Debtor.
(ii) Copies of bills raised and recoveries that were made from tenants.
(iii) Glenmark Bright Life Case Surgo Overseas and its agreement.
(iv) List of employees with their respective joining date with break-up
of salaries and outstanding dues payable to them.
(v) The status of stationery dues like PF, ESIC and TDS.
(vi) Copies of GSTR-9 and 9C for the Financial Year 2018-19 and 2019-
2020.
(vii) Bank statements in relation to as many as ten banks accounts,
with which the Corporate Debtor having its financial relationship.
(viii) Reconciliation of PVR Ledger account.

9 of 18

(ix) Details of other assets like DG set furniture at Empress Mall and IT
Park
(x) Details of Deposit – HPCL SBU of INR 1.04 crores.
(xi) Details of Security Deposits of INR 1.42 crores.
(xii) FDR Details of INR 3.98 crores.
(xiii) List of all the allottees of the Marol Project along with names of the
allottees and their payment details.
(xiv) GST Login credentials of GSTN registered by suspended
management.
(xv) Identify the Plot No. in revenue records in relation to Sale of land
by Kalameshwar Textile Mills Limited to Satellite Consultancy & Services
Limited for Mall at Kamleshwar Unit.
12.
The Appellant submitted, that owing to the aforesaid details which were
supplied by the Appellant in response to the order of the Tribunal dated
08.06.2022 and 15.09.2022, they have been complying with all the directions
in its full terms and in the best possible manner. Besides that, the Appellant
had always been timely assisting and providing documents and the
information sought by the RP, as and when required and submitted that this
response is based upon the supplying of the documents as detailed
hereinabove, the Suspended Board of Directors and RP were able to provide
details of all
such relevant documents pertaining to
Information
Memorandum, publishing of Form-G for invitation of Expression of Interest,
and the request for resolution plan. The RP was able to get all the support of

10 of 18

valuation of the fixed assets, details of all proceedings, security and financial
assets and on the basis of the request for the resolution plan, that has been
submitted by the Prospective Resolution Applicant and which was duly
approved by the Members of the CoC. It was argued by the Appellant, that its
because of the above facts that the RP had been able to reach to the stage of
making the request for resolution plan and that has been submitted by the
Prospective Resolution Applicant and which was approved by the duly
constituted CoC, hence there would be a presumptive inference that the
Appellant had supplied all the necessary and relevant documents, as it was
called for by the RP and further as it was required to be submitted by the
order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 08.06.2022 and 15.09.2022.
13.
It submitted that because of the implication of the approval of the plan
by the CoC and because of the fact that the suspended board has also given
all the rental receipts since 2016 onwards, which were valid up to 2023, all
contracts, salaries, electricity bills and RP expanses which was too duly paid.
The Appellant contended that all documents which were available within the
premises of the Corporate Debtor and protected, had been supplied and
nothing was suppressed by the Appellant. Apart from the aforesaid response
submitted by the Appellant on 24.06.2023 to the application I.A. No. 350 of
2021, he also referred to other communications made by him on 24.09.2022
wherein he had made the following averments:
“1. Audited Financial Statement for the year 2019-2000
2. Form-26AS for the for the Financial Year 2018-2019
3. Form-26AS for the Financial Year 2019-2020

11 of 18

4. FormGSTR-9 for the Financial Year 17-18.

Please refer to our various e-mail correspondences on the subject
matter wherein we have already provided the necessary
documents.

Sir, we have also provided the details of all the properties, fixed
assets, list of plant and machineries well in advance, which you
have covered the details under RFRP”

14.
Receipt of the above documents was duly endorsed by the RP vide its
endorsement of 24.09.2022 made at 02:50 P.M. Based upon the aforesaid
fact, the Appellant submitted that the action taken in pursuance to the I.A.
No. 350 of 2021 was not sustainable for the reasons being that:

(i) That the Adjudicating Authority while passing the impugned order
didn’t even refer to the list of pending documents allegedly not supplied and
had proceeded to pass the impugned order merely on the basis of statement
of the RP.

(ii) When the proceedings are drawn under Section 19(2) of the I&B
Code, it becomes incumbent upon the Adjudicating Authority, to hear the
application particularly the person against the allegation under Section 19
has been made, looking to all circumstances including the statements and
documents placed on record and then only to come to a conclusion as to
whether there had been any overt act of non-cooperation and non-providing
of the documents. This aspect was missing in the impugned order, which do
not reflect an effective hearing before passing the impugned order, due to not
considering the vital facts and the order being silent on it.

12 of 18

15.
Further, it was argued that if we see the language under Section 19(2)
of the I&B Code, it was not supposed to be utilized as a tool by the RP to act
as an arm-twisting devise for the suspended management, during the CIRP,
and also because it may be possible that despite the fact that all the
documents have been supplied, but still there could be a reasonable
presumption with not material that some of the documents may not be
available with the Appellant, being part of the suspended management and in
these eventualities Section 70 of I&B Code, will come into play to safeguard
against the wrath of an inaction under Section 19. Its important to take note
of that the stage at which action under Section 19(2) was being taken the
plan has already been approved by the CoC and therefore none of the
allegations levelled in the application under Section 19(2) preferred by
the Respondent could be sustained. Because upon approval of plan by
CoC, the logical inference would be that it was considered by CoC only
after all the documents being made available to it.
16.
It’s based upon the aforesaid backdrop, normally the question that falls
for consideration before us is, as to whether at all the applications under
Section 19(2) could at all be initiated with the documents having as directed
had been supplied, and were not available! Whether it could be utilized as a
penal action as against the suspended management and that too in absence
of the careful scrutiny of the documents placed by the Appellant on record.
And even because in the absence of a failure on the part of the party to supply
the documents as called for, if there was any breach, then the statute did

13 of 18

contemplate a recourse under Section 70 of the Code, which was not resorted
to in the instant case, in the eventuality that there would be presumption that
because of the fact that there were no proceedings drawn under Section 17 of
the Code and besides that since the plan was already to be approved by the
CoC, the presumption would be that the Appellant had supplied.
17.
Based upon the aforesaid, when the matter was taken up, it was argued
by the Ld. Counsel for the Appellant, that 17 specific documents which were
required to be filed, those were already shared by the Suspended Directors,
as back as on 24.09.2022 and the same was discussed too in the meeting that
was held between the representative of the suspended board and the RP, as
per the minutes recorded therein in the board’s meeting of 24.09.2022, some
15 specific documents/information were listed and were shown as pending to
be handed over and according to the Appellant, out of list of 15 documents,
14 such documents were already handed over to the RP, as the Appellant filed
the affidavit is that regard on 24.06.2023.
18.
There has been nothing on record that was brought by the RP, to show
as to why the RP requires the document, and their relevancy after approval of
plan, which is alleged to have not been supplied. There was no plausible reply
forthcoming, as it was simply answered, that these documents were required
to be handed over to the Successful Resolution Applicant after the approval
of the resolution plan. Though there was no such corresponding need was
ever expressed by the SRA for getting those documents, which had formed the
basis of filing an application under Section 19(2) of the Code, if at all the SRA

14 of 18

had reflected, that the SRA required the documents even after having been
determined as to be a SRA. A tabulation was called for to provide as to which
documents referred to in I.A. No. 350 of 2021 were not supplied. There was
no plausible reply given by the Respondent, as to which documents were not
supplied and as to how they were relevant, in the absence of the same, being
supplied to the SRA as argued by the Ld. Counsel for the Respondent.
19.
The RP submitted, that he had filed another affidavit before the Ld.
Adjudicating Authority on 06.03.2024 along with another list of documents
and information, that was required as on 06.03.2024, the impugned order is
based upon the said list of 06.03.2024. Even during the course of pendency
of this Appeal. This Appellate Tribunal by an order of 18.02.2026 directed the
RP, to share with the Appellant a copy of the statement dated 14.04.2024 and
the Appellant was required to prepare a tabulation-wise explanation with
reference to the dates and figures and RP was also required to make the
statement not general, but in an absolute precision as regards to the
documents these were not supplied; its relevance to the proceedings and its
relevancy of being served to the resolution applicant after approval of plan.
But by an order of 18.02.2026 passed by this Tribunal, it was observed that
RP had continued to receive notice of litigation but without any specific
reference to those proceedings, he submitted that he was not in possession to
place the statement about the documents and their requirement as referred
to hereinabove, and how it were necessary to be supplied to the SRA.

15 of 18

20.
On this premise, the Ld. Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned
order dated 11.06.2024 in I.A. No. 350 of 2021, which was filed under Section
19(2) read with Section 60(5) of the Code. It recorded that the suspended
management had not complied with the order dated 16.04.2024 for providing
the documents sought by the RP, that the statements made on its behalf were
found to be wrong, and that it had not extended cooperation, as seen from the
list of documents yet to be submitted. It then passed the following order:

“In view of the wrong submissions and matter of Section 19
continued, a cost of Rs.25,000/- to be imposed upon respondent
no.1 & 2 each to be paid to Prime Minister's National Relief Fund.
Respondent No. 1 & 2 are directed to appear with all documents
needed by the Resolution Professional on next date of hearing.”

21.
Before we could carve out the reasons from the logic assigned is the
impugned order of 11.06.2024, a reference to Section 19(2) of the Code
becomes necessary to be considered under Section 19(2) reads as under:
“Where any personnel of the corporate debtor, its promoter or any
other person required to assist or cooperate with the interim
resolution professional does not assist or cooperate, the interim
resolution professional may make an application to the
Adjudicating Authority for necessary directions.”

22.
Section 19 obliges the personnel of the Corporate Debtor and the
suspended management to assist and cooperate with the RP. Where they do
not, Section 19(2) allows the RP to apply to the Adjudicating Authority for
directions. The Appellant contends that the information sought was supplied,
as shown by the responses of 24.06.2023 and 14.04.2024, and that Section
19(2) does not permit the imposition of costs. The question, therefore, is
whether the cost imposed by the impugned order can be sustained.

16 of 18

23.
The Appellant also contends that, since the CoC approved the
resolution plan, it must be presumed that the documents supplied were
sufficient. We do not agree. Approval of a plan by the CoC is a commercial
decision. It raises no presumption that the suspended management has
cooperated with the RP. The CIRP may proceed on information which the RP
gathers from other sources, but that does not relieve the suspended
management of its duty.
24.
The Appellant next contends that the only remedy for non-cooperation
lies under Section 70 of the Code. We do not agree. Section 70 provides for
punishment for misconduct in the course of CIRP. It does not take away the
power of the Adjudicating Authority to impose costs on a party for its conduct
in the proceedings before it.

25.
The Appellant relies on the affidavit of 24.06.2023 and the list of
14.04.2024. The RP, by his affidavit dated 06.03.2024, placed on record a list
of the documents and information still outstanding, and the impugned order
is based on that list. The Adjudicating Authority found that the statement
made by the Appellant was not correct and that the documents sought by the
RP had not been provided. We see no reason to differ. The pendency of the
plan for approval did not relieve the Appellant of the duty to hand over the
records of the Corporate Debtor.
26.
We accept that Section 19(2) only enables the RP to seek directions, and
does not provide for the imposition of costs. It was, therefore, not the

17 of 18

appropriate provision, and the appropriate provision ought to have been
invoked. However, the invocation of a wrong provision does not vitiate an order
when the power exercised exists in law. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in P.K.
Palanisamy v. N. Arumugham & Anr. (Civil Appeal arising out of SLP (Civil) No.
2308 of 2009, decided on 23.07.2009) has held that “mentioning of a wrong
provision or non-mentioning of a provision does not invalidate an order if the
court and/or statutory authority had the requisite jurisdiction therefor.” In
doing so, it relied upon its earlier judgment in Ram Sunder Ram v. Union of
India & Ors., (2007) 13 SCC 255, where it was held that a reference to a wrong
provision of law does not by itself vitiate the exercise of a power, “so long as
the power does exist and can be traced to a source available in law”. In that
case, the reference to Section 20 of the Army Act, 1950, instead of Section 22,
was held not to take away the jurisdiction of the authority under Section 22.
Here, the power of the Adjudicating Authority to impose costs on a party for
its conduct in the proceedings before it is traceable to Section 60(5) of the
Code read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. The reference to Section
19(2), therefore, does not by itself invalidate the impugned order. Having gone
through the merits of the case, we find that the Appellant did not cooperate
with the RP. Directions for supply of documents were issued on 08.06.2022
and 15.09.2022. The Ld. Adjudicating Authority found that the documents
had not been provided and that the statement of the Appellant was not
correct. The duty to cooperate under Section 19(1) is a continuing one, and
partial compliance is not full compliance. The cost of Rs. 25,000/- is,

18 of 18

therefore, justified. The Company Appeal is dismissed, and the impugned
order dated 11.06.2024 passed on I.A. No. 350 of 2021 by NCLT, Ahmedabad,
is upheld.
27.
All pending interlocutory applications would stand closed.

[Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma]
Member (Judicial)

New Delhi.
30 Oct, 2026.
Abhishek Pandey
[Arun Baroka]
Member (Technical)

21.
Before we could carve out the reasons from the logic assigned is the
impugned order of 11.06.2024, a reference to Section 19(2) of the Code
becomes necessary to be considered under Section 19(2) reads as under:
“Where any personnel of the corporate debtor, its promoter or any
other person required to assist or cooperate with the interim
resolution professional does not assist or cooperate, the interim
resolution professional may make an application to the
Adjudicating Authority for necessary directions.”

22.
Section 19 obliges the personnel of the Corporate Debtor and the
suspended management to assist and cooperate with the RP. Where they do
not, Section 19(2) allows the RP to apply to the Adjudicating Authority for
directions. The Appellant contends that the information sought was supplied,
as shown by the responses of 24.06.2023 and 14.04.2024, and that Section
19(2) does not permit the imposition of costs. The question, therefore, is
whether the cost imposed by the impugned order can be sustained.

[PAGE 16]
16 of 18

23.
The Appellant also contends that, since the CoC approved the
resolution plan, it must be presumed that the documents supplied were
sufficient. We do not agree. Approval of a plan by the CoC is a commercial
decision. It raises no presumption that the suspended management has
cooperated with the RP. The CIRP may proceed on information which the RP
gathers from other sources, but that does not relieve the suspended
management of its duty.
24.
The Appellant next contends that the only remedy for non-cooperation
lies under Section 70 of the Code. We do not agree. Section 70 provides for
punishment for misconduct in the course of CIRP. It does not take away the
power of the Adjudicating Authority to impose costs on a party for its conduct
in the proceedings before it.

25.
The Appellant relies on the affidavit of 24.06.2023 and the list of
14.04.2024. The RP, by his affidavit dated 06.03.2024, placed on record a list
of the documents and information still outstanding, and the impugned order
is based on that list. The Adjudicating Authority found that the statement
made by the Appellant was not correct and that the documents sought by the
RP had not been provided. We see no reason to differ. The pendency of the
plan for approval did not relieve the Appellant of the duty to hand over the
records of the Corporate Debtor.
26.
We accept that Section 19(2) only enables the RP to seek directions, and
does not provide for the imposition of costs. It was, therefore, not the

[PAGE 17]
17 of 18

appropriate provision, and the appropriate provision ought to have been
invoked. However, the invocation of a wrong provision does not vitiate an order
when the power exercised exists in law. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in P.K.
Palanisamy v. N. Arumugham & Anr. (Civil Appeal arising out of SLP (Civil) No.
2308 of 2009, decided on 23.07.2009) has held that “mentioning of a wrong
provision or non-mentioning of a provision does not invalidate an order if the
court and/or statutory authority had the requisite jurisdiction therefor.” In
doing so, it relied upon its earlier judgment in Ram Sunder Ram v. Union of
India & Ors., (2007) 13 SCC 255, where it was held that a reference to a wrong
provision of law does not by itself vitiate the exercise of a power, “so long as
the power does exist and can be traced to a source available in law”. In that
case, the reference to Section 20 of the Army Act, 1950, instead of Section 22,
was held not to take away the jurisdiction of the authority under Section 22.
Here, the power of the Adjudicating Authority to impose costs on a party for
its conduct in the proceedings before it is traceable to Section 60(5) of the
Code read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. The reference to Section
19(2), therefore, does not by itself invalidate the impugned order. Having gone
through the merits of the case, we find that the Appellant did not cooperate
with the RP. Directions for supply of documents were issued on 08.06.2022
and 15.09.2022. The Ld. Adjudicating Authority found that the documents
had not been provided and that the statement of the Appellant was not
correct. The duty to cooperate under Section 19(1) is a continuing one, and
partial compliance is not full compliance. The cost of Rs. 25,000/- is,

[PAGE 18]
18 of 18

therefore, justified. The Company Appeal is dismissed, and the impugned
order dated 11.06.2024 passed on I.A. No. 350 of 2021 by NCLT, Ahmedabad,
is upheld.
